title: Indigenous methods of measurement
competency: Explain measurement and describe indigenous methods of measuring length, mass, time and volume.

keywords.def: Finding the size of a quantity by comparing it with an agreed standard.
A way of measuring practised locally for a long time and passed from generation to generation.

en.text: Measurement is finding the size of a quantity by comparing it with an agreed standard. Ethiopians have long measured length with the body: hand-span, digit, cubit, foot, pace and arm span. Body units differ from person to person, so they are not standard.

am.text: ልኬት የአንድን መጠን ትልቅነት ከተስማማንበት መለኪያ ጋር በማነጻጸር ማግኘት ነው። ሀገር በቀል የርዝመት መለኪያዎች ስንዝር፣ ጣት፣ ክንድ፣ እግር፣ እርምጃና ዘርጋ ናቸው።

screens.title: Same desk, different answers
screens.ask: Abebe and his little sister both measure the same desk with their hand-span. Will they get the same number?
opts: No, their hands are different sizes
screens.after: No. Her hand-span is shorter, so she counts more spans for the same desk. Body measures are not standard.
screens.best: No, their hands are different sizes

screens.title: Measurement
paras: How big is an object? How tall are you? To answer, we measure.
Measurement is the process of obtaining the magnitude of a quantity relative to an agreed standard.
The indigenous method is practised locally. The modern method is used by the scientific community.

screens.title: Figure 1.1: indigenous units of length
screens.ask: Tap each unit to see how it is measured.
items: From the tip of the little finger to the tip of the thumb, hand stretched out.
The width of an adult man's fingertip.
From the tip of the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.
From the back of the heel to the tip of the big toe.
The length of a person's walking step, measured heel to heel.
Also called fathom: fingertip to fingertip with both arms stretched out.

screens.title: Activity 1.1: one desk, many hand-spans
screens.note: Move the slider from a child's span (about 12 cm) to an adult's (about 24 cm). The desk stays the same, but the count changes. A body unit is not standard.

screens.title: Indigenous methods
paras: An indigenous method of measurement is practised locally for a long time.
It is passed from generation to generation.
Length is the distance between two points. In Ethiopia we use body parts to measure it.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Finding the size of a quantity by comparing it with an agreed standard.
A way of measuring practised locally for a long time and passed from generation to generation.

screens.text: Indigenous length units: which one is measured from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger?
screens.why:
A cubit runs along your forearm.
It starts at the tip of the elbow.
It ends at the tip of the middle finger.
So the answer is cubit.
A hand-span is thumb tip to little-finger tip, not elbow to finger.

screens.text: Activity 1.1, body units: students measure a desk with hand-spans. Why do they get different results?
opts: Their hands are different sizes, so the unit is not standard
screens.ans: Their hands are different sizes, so the unit is not standard
screens.why:
Each student uses their own hand as the unit.
Hands are different sizes.
A small hand fits more times along the desk.
So the counts differ: a hand-span is not a standard unit.
screens.clue: Is everyone's hand the same size?

screens.text: Indigenous length units: put them in order, from shortest to longest.
screens.why:
Compare rough sizes for an adult.
Digit: about 2 cm, one fingertip wide.
Hand-span: about 20 cm. Foot: about 25 cm.
Cubit: about 45 cm.
Arm span: about your height.
So: digit → hand-span → foot → cubit → arm span.
screens.clue: Start with the width of one fingertip.

screens.text: Indigenous length units, true or false: an arm span is also called a fathom.
screens.why:
Stretch both arms out wide.
Measure from one fingertip to the other.
This length is the arm span.
The book says it is also called a fathom. So it is true.

screens.text: Body units vs standard units: a tailor in Merkato measures cloth in cubits. A customer says, "Your cubit is longer than mine!" What is the best fix?
opts: Use a metre tape, an agreed standard
screens.ans: Use a metre tape, an agreed standard
screens.why:
A cubit depends on the tailor's own arm.
The customer's arm is a different length.
So the two cubits do not agree.
A metre tape is the same for everyone.
So use a metre tape, an agreed standard.
A hand-span would have the same problem.
screens.clue: Which unit is the same for every person?

en.text: Ethiopian markets use weqet for gold powder, quntal (100 kg) for grain and feresula (17 kg) for pepper and coffee. Elders told the time from the shadow of a tree. Jog, tassa, sini, birchiko and kubaya are cups and cans used to measure volume.

am.text: በገበያ ወቄት ለወርቅ፣ ኩንታል (100 ኪ.ግ) ለእህል፣ ፈረሱላ (17 ኪ.ግ) ለበርበሬና ለቡና ያገለግላሉ። ጊዜ በዛፍ ጥላ ይለካ ነበር።

screens.title: Before clocks
screens.ask: Long ago, how could an elder tell the time of day without a clock?
opts: From the shadow of a tree
From the colour of the soil
screens.after: From the shadow. It is long in the morning and late afternoon and almost gone at noon.
screens.best: From the shadow of a tree

screens.title: Mass
paras: The amount of matter in a substance is called mass.
Weqet measures gold powder in local markets.
Quntal is a bag for grains. It equals 100 kg.
Feresula measures pepper and coffee. It equals 17 kg.

screens.title: Time and volume
paras: Time is the measure of the duration of an interval.
The Sun's position changes, so a tree's shadow changes length.
Volume is the space an object occupies.
In Addis Ababa markets, people measure volume with a jog, tassa, sini, birchiko or kubaya. Tap each one below.

screens.title: Market measures of volume
screens.ask: Tap each tool to see what it is and what it measures.
items: A plastic cup. Used for liquids.
A can. Used for cereals, pulses, liquids and other solids.
A small ceramic cup. Used for coffee, pulses and spices.
A glass. Used for pulses and liquids.
A mug. Used for cereals, pulses and liquids.

screens.title: Market units in kilograms
screens.note: 1 quntal = 100 kg. 1 feresula = 17 kg. Move the sliders to change the number of bags.

screens.title: Key word
defs: A way of measuring practised locally for a long time and passed from generation to generation.

screens.text: Indigenous units: match each unit with what it measures.
screens.why:
Weqet: a small unit for gold powder.
Quntal: a bag for grain, 100 kg.
Feresula: for pepper and coffee, 17 kg.
Sini: a small ceramic cup for coffee, pulses and spices.
screens.clue: Two are for mass of farm goods, one for gold, one is a small cup.

screens.ask: Indigenous mass unit: one quntal = ___ kg
screens.why:
A quntal is a big bag for grain.
The book says 1 quntal = 100 kg.
So the answer is 100.
screens.clue: It is a big bag of grain.

screens.text: Telling time by shadow: when is a tree's shadow shortest?
screens.why:
A shadow is long when the Sun is low.
In the morning and late afternoon the Sun is low.
At noon the Sun is high overhead.
So the shadow is shortest at noon.
At night there is no sunlight, so no shadow.
screens.clue: Where is the Sun at midday?

screens.text: Indigenous volume: what is the main problem with measuring teff in a tassa?
opts: Tassas are not all the same size
Teff cannot go in a can
screens.ans: Tassas are not all the same size
screens.why:
A tassa is a can.
Cans are made in many sizes.
One seller's tassa may hold more than another's.
The teff can also be heaped or levelled.
So a tassa is not an agreed standard.
screens.clue: Is every can made to the same size?

screens.text: Indigenous mass units: a farmer sells 3 quntals of wheat. A trader weighs them on a balance. How much should the balance show?
screens.why:
1 quntal = 100 kg.
The farmer has 3 quntals.
3 × 100 = 300 kg.
Check: 51 kg is 3 feresulas (3 × 17), not 3 quntals.
screens.clue: How many kilograms are in one quntal?

items.text: Indigenous mass units: which one has a fixed value in kilograms?
items.why:
Look for a unit with a number of kilograms.
The book says 1 feresula = 17 kg.
Weqet is for gold, but the book gives it no kg value.
Hand-span measures length; kubaya measures volume.
So the answer is feresula.
items.clue: Look for a unit with a number of kg.

items.text: Indigenous volume measures: which is a problem with them?
opts: The containers are not a standard size
They are only used in labs
items.ans: The containers are not a standard size
items.why:
Market volume tools are cups, cans and mugs.
They come in different sizes.
So "one kubaya" can hold different amounts.
The problem: they are not a standard size.

items.text: Indigenous measurement: sort each point into a pro (a good thing) or a con (a problem).
items: Body parts and cups cost nothing.
They differ from person to person.
Understood by everyone in the market
Hard to convert to SI units
items.why:
Pro: body parts and cups are free and always at hand.
Pro: everyone in the market understands them.
Con: they change from person to person.
Con: they have no fixed value, so they are hard to convert to SI units.
items.clue: Is it a good thing or a problem?

test.text: Definition of measurement: measurement is comparing a quantity with
test.why:
Measuring means finding the size of a quantity.
We compare it with a fixed amount that everyone agrees on.
This is an agreed standard.
A guess or a friend's answer is not fixed.

test.text: Indigenous length units: a digit is
opts: fingertip to fingertip of both arms
test.why:
A digit is the smallest body unit.
It is the width of an adult man's fingertip.
Elbow to fingertip is a cubit.
Fingertip to fingertip of both arms is an arm span.

test.ask: Indigenous mass unit: one feresula = ___ kg
test.why:
A feresula is used for pepper and coffee.
The book gives 1 feresula = 17 kg.
So the answer is 17.

test.text: Indigenous volume: which tool measures volume in the market?
test.why:
A kubaya is a mug.
It holds cereals, pulses or liquids, so it measures volume.
Weqet and quntal measure mass.
A cubit measures length.

test.text: Body units: why are they not reliable?
opts: They change from person to person
test.ans: They change from person to person
test.why:
Body units use a part of a person's body.
Every person's body is a different size.
So one person's cubit is not another's.
There is no agreed standard, so results change.

notes.text: The book numbers only 1.1 and 1.2. Lessons 1.1a–1.1e split section 1.1 at its own headings (Indigenous methods; Physical quantities; Prefixes and conversion; Measuring; Accuracy and precision).
The "Pace" definition contradicts itself: "one normal walking step" vs "heel to heel of the same foot" (two steps). The lesson says "walking step, measured heel to heel".
Activity 1.1 asks for groups of 5 but the table has 4 rows. Projects 1.1–1.2 are research tasks; model answers are in source.md.
